questions.text: Why does this lesson use a canonical Tool and Call representation with provider-specific translators at the edges?

options.A: To make every provider accept exactly the same request JSON.
options.B: To let normalized tool calls bypass host-side argument validation.
options.C: To execute tools inside the provider instead of the host program.
options.D: To keep shared logic independent of provider envelopes and argument encodings.

questions.explanation: Adapters translate provider-specific fields, nesting, and argument encodings while shared application logic uses canonical representations.

questions.text: In the lesson’s offline translator, you must force get_weather when several tools are available. Which Gemini configuration does tool_choice_gemini emit?

options.A: mode AUTO with allowed_function_names set to get_weather.
options.B: mode ANY with allowed_function_names set to get_weather.
options.D: mode NONE with allowed_function_names set to get_weather.

questions.explanation: The force branch combines mode ANY with allowed_function_names containing only the selected tool name.

questions.text: In the supplied parse_openai function, function.arguments is changed from a JSON string to an already-parsed Python dict. What happens at json.loads(fn["arguments"])?

options.A: It raises TypeError because json.loads does not accept a dict.
options.B: It returns the same dict because decoding is idempotent.
options.C: It converts the dict to a JSON string for Call.args.
options.D: It skips the call because its arguments were already decoded.

questions.explanation: json.loads expects a string, bytes, or bytearray. This parser assumes the fixture’s string-encoded arguments and does not handle a dict.
